Q: What should a complete capstone include?
A: Build one scoped assistant with a UI, authenticated API, retrieval, a limited agent, durable business operations, evaluation, tracing, and recovery. Add voice or document AI only when the use case needs it.
Why: Define a small set of useful tasks and publish synthetic fixtures, architecture decisions, and a reproducible local setup.
Risk: Adding many features can hide weak core guarantees.
Trade: Narrow scope is easier to evaluate and may look less broad.
Try: Choose three user journeys and one explicit out-of-scope request before coding.
spoken: A strong capstone includes a scoped use case, requirements and threat model, reproducible setup, tested code, versioned data/evaluation, architecture decisions and demonstrated failure recovery. Separate implemented behavior from proposals and leave a clear list of known limitations.

misconception_target: A capstone is just a working demo

Documented quality metrics for the built system

production_case: Another engineer starts from a clean environment, reproduces an unauthorized-access negative case and a lost-ack retry, inspects durable effects and reads the measured quality/latency trade-offs.
complexity: Estimate development and runtime resources from concrete workload and delivery requirements. Counting project phases is not a meaningful algorithmic complexity analysis.

follow_ups.Q: What makes a capstone stronger than a polished chat demo?
follow_ups.A: Independent evidence of correctness, permissions and recovery under failure, plus an explanation of assumptions and trade-offs.

Q: How should the learning journey be sequenced?
A: Learn backend and data fundamentals, retrieval and evidence, agent tool use, context and prompts, durable orchestration, evaluation, then multimodal and live delivery. Revisit earlier layers as failures emerge.
Why: Build a working increment at each stage and defend its design trade-offs. The roadmap is a dependency path, not a fixed calendar guarantee.
Risk: Reading all chapters without implementing leaves integration gaps undiscovered.
Trade: Incremental projects take more setup and produce stronger understanding.
Try: Map each chapter to one artifact or demonstrated behavior.

Q: What should a public portfolio say about AI assistance?
A: Explain your role in design, implementation, review, and validation, including where AI helped. Claims of competence should be supported by decisions and working evidence.
Why: Publish a short engineering log describing a failure you found, how you diagnosed it, and how you verified the fix.
Risk: Presenting generated explanations as verified production results undermines trust.
Trade: Transparency may reveal limits and makes your work easier to assess.
Try: Write a project description separating demonstrated behavior from planned extensions.

Q: How should project documentation be structured?
A: Lead with the user problem, supported tasks, architecture, setup, operating constraints, evaluation results, and known limitations. Link deeper explanations from this overview.
Why: Keep commands reproducible with synthetic data and clearly scoped dependency versions. Show one success and one failure walkthrough.
Risk: A large README without a runnable path can make a strong project hard to assess.
Trade: Concise onboarding requires separate detail pages and improves accessibility.
Try: Ask a new reader to run one task without verbal guidance.

Q: Which measurements belong in a portfolio report?
A: Report task completion, unsupported-answer rate, authorization invariants, recovery outcomes, p95 latency, and cost under a described workload. Include dataset size and environment.
Why: Distinguish measured numbers from targets and estimates. Retain configuration and release IDs so a comparison can be reproduced.
Risk: Benchmark claims without task mix or hardware context are difficult to interpret.
Trade: Honest limitations may look less impressive and provide credible evidence.
Try: Publish a small result table with a baseline, one improvement, and one regression.

Q: How should an architecture decision record be written?
A: Describe the concrete problem, constraints, considered options, chosen approach, consequences, and conditions that would trigger reconsideration. Keep it tied to evidence.
Why: For example, justify SSE over WebSockets through message direction and reconnect needs rather than popularity.
Risk: A retrospective justification can conceal alternatives that were never evaluated.
Trade: Decision records cost time and preserve engineering context.
Try: Write one record for transaction ownership and one for agent orchestration.

Q: How should a capstone release be secured?
A: Remove secrets and customer data, constrain tools and outbound access, validate identity and ownership, and isolate evaluation side effects. Include dependency and artifact provenance.
Why: Use a reviewed deployment manifest and a rollback path. Keep administrative actions separate from ordinary agent capabilities.
Risk: A public demo can expose backend endpoints even if the repository is private.
Trade: Hardened deployment adds friction and supports credible public access.
Try: Threat-model the demo as an anonymous user and an authenticated malicious user.

Q: How should interviews use the roadmap?
A: Explain a complete journey, then zoom into one failure boundary and defend a trade-off. Use diagrams and actual measurements to distinguish understanding from terminology recall.
Why: Practice concise answers first, then expand into transaction scope, context design, permissions, and evaluation when asked.
Risk: Memorized framework definitions do not demonstrate reasoning under changed constraints.
Trade: Deep specialization reduces breadth and produces stronger technical discussions.
Try: Answer how your design changes when traffic grows tenfold or a provider fails.

Q: What should completion of a chapter mean?
A: You can explain the mechanism, implement a small example, reproduce a relevant failure, and justify a trade-off. A learned checkbox is a personal study signal.
Why: Use the chapter lab acceptance criteria and write your own explanation before revealing the detailed answer.
Risk: Marking everything complete without independent work gives misleading progress.
Trade: Higher standards slow apparent progress and deepen practical competence.
Try: Revisit one learned topic and solve its exercise without viewing the answer.

Q: How should the roadmap continue after the capstone?
A: Choose a real weakness revealed by evaluation: retrieval quality, multilingual behavior, privacy, latency, model serving, accessibility, or operational recovery. Deepen that area with a controlled experiment.
Why: Keep a baseline and compare one intervention at a time. Add a new framework only when it solves a defined problem.
Risk: Collecting technologies can fragment the system without improving user outcomes.
Trade: Focused depth limits feature count and builds durable engineering judgment.
Try: Propose your next experiment with a hypothesis, dataset, metric, budget, and stopping rule.
